  • Market segmentation is the process of dividing a broad consumer market into sub-groups based on
  • shared characteristics. The four broad bases for segmenting the consumer market are
  • A. Geographic Segmentation
  • Geographic segmentation refers to divide markets based on geography. customers’ geographic criteria
  • can significantly affect their needs as consumers. This divides the market based on location such as
  • region, city, climate, or population density. Consumers from different geographic areas have varying
  • needs. .
  • Geographic segmentation elements include
  • Region or area, such as country, state, province, county, town or city
  • Size, such as population or population density.
  • Climate, such as weather patterns
  • Example
  • LG Electronics, the leading electrical appliances company markets for its heaters in cold geographical
  • areas whereas the same company markets for Air Conditioners in hot geographical areas.
  • A clothing brand offering woollen garments in North India during winter and light cotton clothes in
  • South India due to hot weather.
  • B. Demographic Segmentation
  • The most common way to identify a consumer market is by demographic segmentation, which refers to
  • the criteria most businesses use to understand how groups of their target market are different from one
  • another. This is one of the widest market segmentation, marketers divide customer population based on
  • different variables in this segmentation. This is based on age, gender, income, education, occupation
  • religion, and family size, etc. Segmenting your target market by demographics is essential because these
  • criteria affect their individual needs. For example, a man in his early 30s has different preferences than a
  • woman in her late 60s. If your business sells shoes, you cannot appeal to both demographic segments in
  • the same way. The young man may be interested in athletic name-brand shoes, while the older woman
  • may want comfortable sandals with arch support.
  • The criteria for demographic segmentation includes
  • Gender , Age, Family status, Sexual orientation, Occupation, Income, Education, Religion, Ethnicity
  • Nationality
  • Example: Hindustan Unilever markets Fair & Lovely (now Glow & Lovely) targeted mainly towards
  • women in the middle-income group. Kelloggs that offers different cereal brands for kids and adults
  • healthy eaters and weight watchers, etc.
  • C. Psychographic Segmentation
  • Psychographic segmentation considers the psychological aspect of how the potential customer responds
  • to a product. This type of market segmentation targets the lifestyle, activities, interests and opinions of
  • potential customers. People within the same demographic group can exhibit very different psychographic
  • profiles. A consumer’s psychographic qualities affect which products and services they buy. Consumer’s
  • interests and activities determine the products and services they buy. By understanding a segment's
  • values, attitudes, interests and activities, businesses can market the right products to them in the right
  • way. Some of the psychographic bases of segmentation.
  •  Values, such as what they believe to be important to them, including family, community, money
  • or success.
  •  Attitudes and opinions, such as how they feel about a political party or toward a key social issue.
  • Some consumers only support companies that are in line with their political or social beliefs.
  •  Interests, such as what kinds of movies they watch or what their hobbies are.
  •  Activities, such as whether they play a sport or instrument or enjoy a cooking a particular kind of
  • cuisine
  •  Social class.
  •  Lifestyle
  •  Personality
  • Example: Titan’s Fastrack targets the young, adventurous and fun-loving youth segment. Mountain Dew
  • uses a marketing strategy that promotes its product by associating masculinity and a daring personality
  • with the brand's drinkers, targeting young individuals who crave such a personality and associate
  • themselves with it.
  • D. Behavioural Segmentation
  • Behavioural segmentation refers to customer segmentation based on how they use, behave or make
  • decisions related to a product. Behavioural segmentation includes
  •  Benefits consumers are looking for from the product
  •  Whether they have previously bought the product
  •  How often they need the product or how often they use the product
  •  How ready they are to buy the product right now
  •  Whether they feel loyal toward your brand
  •  When they buy the product, such as on holidays or for specific milestones.
  • In this category, the following bases are adopted to segment the markets.
  •  Occasions: Buyers can be distinguished according to occasions when they get the idea of buying or
  • make a purchase or use a product. For example, tourist travel is influenced by occasions related to
  • festivals, vacations, etc. A tourist bus Operator can specialise in serving people during one of these
  • occasions.
  •  User status: Such as non-users, ex-users, potential. users, first-time users and regular users.
  •  Usage rate: Markets can also be segmented on the basis of extent of usage of the product as light
  • medium, and heavy user groups.
  •  Loyalty status: A market can also be segments by consumer loyalty patterns. Loyalty status. Includes
  • Hardcore loyalists who buy one brand all the time, Soft-core loyalist who are loyal to two or three
  • brands all the time, Shifting loyalists who shift from one brand to another., Switchers who show no
  • loyalty to any brand.
  •  Type of Buying Situations: Three types of buying situations: 1) new buy, 2) modified buy, and 3)
  • straight re-buy.

  • The Stimulus-Response Model in marketing explains how external marketing stimuli and other factors
  • influence a consumer’s buying behaviour. It includes the following components
  • Components of the Stimulus-Response Model
  • Response (Output)
  • This is the result of the decision-making process and shows how the consumer responds to the stimuli.
  •  Key Responses
  • o Product choice.
  • o Brand choice.
  • o Purchase timing.
  • o Purchase frequency.
  •  Example: The consumer purchases a smartphone after seeing an ad and evaluating alternatives.
  • Example of the Stimulus-Response Model in Action
  •  Stimuli: A 20% discount on a popular smartphone is advertised through social media.
  •  Black Box: The consumer evaluates whether the smartphone satisfies their need for better
  • photography and affordability.
  •  Response: The consumer buys the smartphone, feeling confident it meets their requirements.
  • This model emphasizes the importance of understanding what influences consumers to act and helps
  • marketers design strategies to stimulate desired responses.
  • Example
  • A customer sees an Instagram ad (promotion – marketing stimulus) for a new herbal shampoo that is eco
  • friendly (aligned with cultural values – environmental stimulus). They consider their need for chemical
  • free hair care (black box), compare it with other brands, and decide to buy the shampoo online (buyer
  • response).
